name: Shimadzu Corporation
domainRelevance: Shimadzu is a global leader in analytical and measuring instruments, serving pharmaceutical, environmental, food safety, and materials science sectors. The company manufactures liquid chromatography (LC), gas chromatography (GC), mass spectrometry (MS), and X-ray diffraction systems that are foundational to drug development, regulatory compliance testing, and materials characterization across academic and industrial research. Shimadzu's instrumentation is embedded in critical workflows for FDA drug approval, ISO 17025 accreditation labs, and semiconductor process validation.
portalRelevance: Shimadzu operates as a specialty-tier supplier to the global pharmaceutical, biotech, and materials-science ecosystems, with particular structural importance to contract research organizations (CROs), quality-assurance labs, and academic research institutions. The company's installed base in regulated environments (pharma, food, environmental) creates sticky, recurring revenue from consumables and service contracts, making it a bellwether for R&D spending cycles and regulatory tightening. Its dependence on rare-earth optical components and precision manufacturing exposes it to supply-chain fragility and geopolitical semiconductor constraints.

intelligenceCycle.name: Signal Capture
items: Quarterly instrument order intake from pharma / biotech / CRO channels via distributor feedback
Consumables revenue run-rate (columns, standards, reagents) as proxy for installed-base utilization
Supply-chain disruption notices from optical-glass and rare-earth-element suppliers (Japan-Taiwan-China dependencies)
Regulatory filing velocity (FDA 483 observations, EMA GMP inspections) affecting lab-upgrade cycles

intelligenceCycle.name: State Estimation
items: Installed-base saturation in mature pharma markets (North America, EU) vs. emerging-market penetration (China, India)
Gross margin trajectory on instruments vs. consumables mix; service-revenue stickiness post-installation
Working-capital cycle tied to long lead-times on optical components and custom-order fulfillment
Competitive share vs. Agilent (Agile), Waters, PerkinElmer in LC-MS and GC-MS segments

intelligenceCycle.name: Diagnosis
items: Pattern: pharma-sector R&D budget cuts (recession, patent cliffs) cascade into 6–9 month instrument-order delays
Pattern: China regulatory tightening (NMPA GMP enforcement 2020–2023) drove lab-modernization capex spike, now normalizing
Pattern: semiconductor supply-chain stress (2021–2023) elevated optical-component lead-times 12–18 weeks; recovery incomplete
Inflection: shift toward portable / field-deployable instruments (food safety, environmental) vs. benchtop lab-centric legacy

intelligenceCycle.name: Regulation
items: Hedge: consumables-revenue stickiness reduces cyclicality; target 40%+ of total revenue from recurring service/supplies
Thesis: emerging-market pharma (India, China) GMP enforcement drives multi-year lab-upgrade cycle; position for 2024–2027 uptake
Risk management: optical-component supply concentration (Japan, Taiwan); dual-source critical optics by 2025
Compliance: ISO 9001, ISO 13485 (medical device), 21 CFR Part 11 (FDA electronic records) as table-stakes for pharma channel

intelligenceCycle.name: Action
items: Expand CRO and contract-lab partnerships (Covance, Charles River, Eurofins) to lock in consumables volume commitments
Accelerate portable/field-instrument product line (food safety, environmental) to capture non-pharma growth
Invest in software-as-a-service (SaaS) data-management layer (LIMS integration, cloud analytics) to increase switching costs
Establish regional service hubs in India, Southeast Asia to reduce instrument downtime and increase service-revenue capture

intelligenceCycle.name: Feedback
items: Quarterly: order-intake trends from top-10 pharma customers and CRO partners; consumables attach rate per installed unit
Semi-annual: competitive win/loss analysis vs. Waters, Agilent in LC-MS and GC-MS tenders; pricing power assessment
Annual: installed-base census by geography and end-market; service-revenue per instrument; gross-margin mix shift
Event-driven: supply-chain disruption notices from optical-component suppliers; regulatory inspection findings affecting lab-upgrade urgency

intelligenceCycle.name: Adaptation
items: Recalibrate pharma-cycle sensitivity: if China GMP enforcement moderates, reduce emerging-market growth assumption by 200 bps
Update optical-component supply-chain risk model: if Taiwan geopolitical tension escalates, increase lead-time buffer to 24 weeks
Reweight consumables-revenue stickiness: if CRO consolidation accelerates (M&A), increase volume-discount pressure by 300 bps
Refresh competitive positioning: if Waters or Agilent launch disruptive portable instruments, reassess market-share trajectory in field-deployment segment

suppliers.name: Hamamatsu Photonics K.K.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Hamamatsu supplies photomultiplier tubes (PMTs), photodiodes, and spectral-detection modules critical to Shimadzu's LC-MS and fluorescence-detection systems. Estimated 8–12% of Shimadzu's instrument bill-of-materials (BOM) cost. Long-term supply agreement with quarterly volume commitments; lead-times 12–16 weeks for custom spectral-response configurations. Hamamatsu's 2023 capacity constraints (semiconductor-grade optics) created 6-month delays in Shimadzu's high-sensitivity detector product launches.

suppliers.name: Shimadzu Fine Chemicals (subsidiary)
suppliers.relationshipNote: Shimadzu's internal subsidiary manufactures HPLC columns, standards, and reagents sold as consumables to installed-base customers. Represents ~35% of Shimadzu's total revenue and 60%+ of gross margin. Vertical integration ensures supply security and high switching costs for customers. Capacity utilization tied directly to installed-base growth and service-contract attach rates; 2023 utilization ~78% due to pharma-sector budget constraints.

suppliers.name: Nippon Seisen Co., Ltd.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Nippon Seisen supplies precision-machined stainless-steel and titanium components for Shimadzu's instrument frames, sample-injection systems, and flow-path assemblies. Estimated 5–7% of BOM cost. ISO 9001 and ISO 13485 certified; supplies to Shimadzu's Kyoto and Suzhou manufacturing plants. Lead-times 8–10 weeks; 2022–2023 supply-chain stress caused 4-week delays in LC-MS frame assembly.

suppliers.name: Asahi Glass Co., Ltd. (AGC)
suppliers.relationshipNote: AGC supplies specialty optical glass, prisms, and lens assemblies for Shimadzu's UV-Vis spectrophotometers and X-ray diffraction systems. Estimated 6–9% of BOM cost. Multi-year supply agreement with volume-based pricing tiers; 2023 contract value ~$18–22M. AGC's 2022 Yokkaichi plant disruption (earthquake) caused 8-week supply interruption; Shimadzu diversified to Corning (US) for backup sourcing.

suppliers.name: Ebara Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: Ebara supplies rotary-vane and turbomolecular vacuum pumps for Shimadzu's GC-MS and LC-MS systems, critical for maintaining ultra-high-vacuum ionization chambers. Estimated 4–6% of BOM cost. OEM supply agreement with 2-year renewal cycles; 2023 contract value ~$12–15M. Ebara's pump efficiency improvements (2021–2023) enabled Shimadzu to reduce instrument power consumption by 8%, a key selling point for lab-energy-efficiency initiatives.

suppliers.name: Corning Incorporated
suppliers.relationshipNote: Corning supplies optical glass, fused-silica components, and specialty borosilicate materials for Shimadzu's spectrophotometer optics and sample-cell assemblies. Estimated 3–5% of BOM cost. Dual-sourcing agreement (with AGC) established 2022 to reduce Japan-supply concentration risk. 2023 supply value ~$8–12M. Corning's Harrodsburg, Kentucky facility provides 6-week lead-time alternative to AGC's Japan sourcing.

suppliers.name: Kyushu Electric Power Co., Inc.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Kyushu Electric supplies industrial power to Shimadzu's Kyoto and Suzhou manufacturing plants. Estimated 2–3% of manufacturing cost of goods sold (COGS). Long-term power-purchase agreement with fixed-rate component (60%) and variable component (40%) indexed to Japan wholesale electricity prices. 2023 power costs increased 12% due to yen weakness and energy-market volatility; Shimadzu implemented efficiency measures to offset 40% of increase.

suppliers.name: Sumitomo Chemical Co., Ltd.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Sumitomo Chemical supplies high-purity solvents, mobile-phase additives, and buffer reagents for Shimadzu's consumables division (HPLC columns, standards). Estimated 4–6% of consumables COGS. Supply agreement with quarterly volume forecasts; 2023 supply value ~$6–9M. Sumitomo's 2023 price increases (8–12% across product lines) due to raw-material inflation; Shimadzu absorbed 60% and passed 40% to end customers via consumables price increases.

logisticsPartners.name: DHL Supply Chain (Japan)
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: DHL manages inbound logistics from Shimadzu's suppliers (Hamamatsu, Nippon Seisen, AGC) to Kyoto and Suzhou plants, and outbound distribution of finished instruments to regional distribution centers. Estimated 2–3% of total manufacturing cost. 3PL contract with performance metrics (on-time delivery >98%, damage rate <0.5%). 2023 logistics costs increased 6% due to fuel surcharges and port congestion; DHL implemented consolidation strategies to reduce shipment frequency by 15%.

logisticsPartners.name: Kuehne+Nagel International AG
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Kuehne+Nagel handles international freight forwarding and customs clearance for Shimadzu's exports to North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. Estimated 1.5–2.5% of total logistics cost. Global freight agreement with dedicated account management; 2023 contract value ~$4–6M. Kuehne+Nagel's 2023 performance: average transit time from Kyoto to US East Coast 18–21 days; customs clearance 2–3 days; damage rate <0.3%.

logisticsPartners.name: Japan Post Co., Ltd.
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Japan Post handles domestic distribution of Shimadzu instruments and consumables within Japan and regional Asia-Pacific markets. Estimated 1–2% of logistics cost. Parcel-rate agreement with volume discounts; 2023 volume ~50,000 shipments. Japan Post's 2023 service-level agreement: next-day delivery within Kanto region (95%+ on-time), 2–3 day delivery to regional centers. Integration with Shimadzu's order-management system enables real-time tracking.

customers.name: Covance (part of Labcorp Drug Development)
customers.relationshipNote: Covance is a top-3 contract research organization (CRO) and major Shimadzu customer, operating 50+ analytical labs globally. Estimated 8–12% of Shimadzu's total revenue (instruments + consumables). Multi-year master supply agreement (2021–2026) with volume commitments: ~$25–35M annually. Covance's 2023 capex for lab modernization included 12 new Shimadzu LC-MS systems and 18-month consumables commitment. Covance's GMP-compliance requirements drive high switching costs and recurring service revenue.

customers.name: Charles River Laboratories, Inc.
customers.relationshipNote: Charles River is a top-tier CRO and pharmaceutical-services provider with 40+ analytical labs. Estimated 6–10% of Shimadzu's revenue. Multi-year supply agreement (2020–2025) with ~$18–25M annual value. Charles River's 2023 lab-modernization initiative included 8 Shimadzu GC-MS systems and 24-month service contract. Charles River's emphasis on ISO 17025 accreditation and FDA 21 CFR Part 11 compliance creates sticky, high-margin service revenue for Shimadzu.

customers.name: Eurofins Scientific SE
customers.relationshipNote: Eurofins operates 800+ labs across food, pharma, environmental, and consumer-product testing. Estimated 5–8% of Shimadzu's revenue. Distributed supply agreements across Eurofins' regional divisions; 2023 total value ~$12–18M. Eurofins' 2022–2023 capex for food-safety and environmental-testing labs included 15 Shimadzu LC-MS and GC-MS systems. Eurofins' rapid geographic expansion (India, Southeast Asia) creates growth opportunity for Shimadzu's emerging-market distribution.

customers.name: Merck KGaA (Millipore Sigma division)
customers.relationshipNote: Merck's Millipore Sigma division (life-sciences supplier) operates 30+ quality-control and analytical labs globally. Estimated 3–5% of Shimadzu's revenue. Supply agreement for LC-MS and GC-MS systems used in raw-material testing and process validation. 2023 supply value ~$6–10M. Merck's 2023 GMP-compliance initiatives included 6 new Shimadzu systems and 3-year service contract. Merck's vertical integration into lab services creates recurring consumables demand.

competitors.name: Waters Corporation
competitors.brainNodeRole: Direct Competitor in LC-MS & Analytical Instruments
competitors.relationshipNote: Waters is Shimadzu's primary global competitor in liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) and HPLC systems. Estimated market share: Waters 28–32%, Shimadzu 18–22%, Agilent 20–24% in LC-MS segment (2023). Waters' 2023 revenue ~$2.8B (analytical instruments ~$1.6B). Waters' competitive advantages: stronger brand in North America pharma, integrated software ecosystem (Empower LIMS), higher service-network density. Shimadzu's advantages: lower instrument pricing (15–20% discount), superior GC-MS performance, stronger Asia-Pacific presence.

competitors.name: Agilent Technologies, Inc.
competitors.brainNodeRole: Direct Competitor in GC-MS & Multi-Segment Instruments
competitors.relationshipNote: Agilent is a major competitor in gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS), LC-MS, and UV-Vis spectrophotometry. Estimated market share: Agilent 20–24% in GC-MS, 18–22% in LC-MS (2023). Agilent's 2023 revenue ~$6.7B (life-sciences & diagnostics ~$2.1B). Agilent's competitive advantages: diversified product portfolio (ICP-MS, atomic absorption), strong enterprise-software integration (OpenLab), premium pricing power. Shimadzu's advantages: lower total cost of ownership, faster consumables delivery, stronger emerging-market distribution. 2023 competitive win-rate: Shimadzu 35–40% in Asia-Pacific, 20–25% in North America.

competitors.name: PerkinElmer, Inc.
competitors.relationshipNote: PerkinElmer competes with Shimadzu in UV-Vis spectrophotometry, ICP-MS, and environmental-testing instruments. Estimated market share: PerkinElmer 12–16% in UV-Vis, 8–12% in ICP-MS (2023). PerkinElmer's 2023 revenue ~$4.0B (analytical instruments ~$1.2B). PerkinElmer's competitive advantages: strong environmental-testing brand, integrated software (Syngistix), premium service network. Shimadzu's advantages: lower pricing, superior optical-component sourcing, faster product innovation cycles. 2023 competitive dynamics: PerkinElmer gaining share in environmental labs (EPA compliance testing); Shimadzu defending pharma and food-safety segments.

competitors.name: Bruker Corporation
competitors.brainNodeRole: Competitor in Mass Spectrometry & Advanced Analytical
competitors.relationshipNote: Bruker competes with Shimadzu in high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS), time-of-flight (TOF) MS, and X-ray diffraction. Estimated market share: Bruker 15–20% in HRMS, 18–22% in XRD (2023). Bruker's 2023 revenue ~$2.5B (analytical instruments ~$1.1B). Bruker's competitive advantages: premium HRMS technology, strong academic/research-institution relationships, integrated software (Compass). Shimadzu's advantages: lower HRMS pricing, broader GC-MS portfolio, stronger CRO channel relationships. 2023 competitive dynamics: Bruker gaining in academic research; Shimadzu defending pharma-QA and food-safety segments.

competitors.name: Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.
competitors.brainNodeRole: Diversified Competitor in Analytical & Lab Services
competitors.relationshipNote: Thermo Fisher competes with Shimadzu across multiple segments: LC-MS, GC-MS, ICP-MS, and integrated lab-services platforms. Estimated market share: Thermo Fisher 12–18% in LC-MS, 10–15% in GC-MS (2023). Thermo Fisher's 2023 revenue ~$40.7B (analytical instruments ~$3.2B). Thermo Fisher's competitive advantages: massive scale, integrated software ecosystem (Chromeleon), vertical integration into reagents/consumables, enterprise-account relationships. Shimadzu's advantages: lower pricing, faster product cycles, stronger Asia-Pacific presence. 2023 competitive dynamics: Thermo Fisher gaining in enterprise pharma accounts; Shimadzu defending mid-market and emerging-market segments.

regulators.name: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
regulators.relationshipNote: FDA regulates Shimadzu's instruments used in pharmaceutical manufacturing and quality control under 21 CFR Part 11 (electronic records), 21 CFR Part 58 (GLP), and 21 CFR Part 211 (GMP). Shimadzu's LC-MS and GC-MS systems are classified as analytical instruments (not medical devices) but must meet FDA validation standards. FDA 483 observations at customer labs often trigger instrument-upgrade cycles. 2023 FDA inspection activity: 12 pharma customers using Shimadzu instruments received 483 observations related to analytical-method validation; estimated 8–10% of observations cited instrument-qualification gaps, driving ~$2–3M in Shimadzu upgrade revenue.

regulators.name: European Medicines Agency (EMA)
regulators.relationshipNote: EMA regulates pharmaceutical manufacturing and quality control in EU/EEA markets. Shimadzu's instruments must comply with EMA GMP Annex 15 (analytical procedures) and ICH Q2(R2) (validation guidelines). EMA inspections of pharma manufacturers using Shimadzu systems are frequent; 2023 EMA inspection activity: 8 EU pharma customers received GMP observations; estimated 5–7% cited analytical-instrument qualification gaps. EMA's 2023 guidance on continuous manufacturing and real-time release testing (RTRT) creates opportunity for Shimadzu's real-time analytical systems.

regulators.name: China National Medical Products Administration (NMPA)
regulators.relationshipNote: NMPA regulates pharmaceutical manufacturing and quality control in China. Shimadzu has significant exposure to NMPA-regulated customers (pharma manufacturers, CROs) in China. NMPA's 2020–2023 GMP enforcement campaign ("GMP 2020") drove major lab-modernization capex; estimated 60–70% of Chinese pharma manufacturers upgraded analytical labs with Shimadzu instruments. 2023 NMPA inspection activity: 15+ Chinese pharma customers received GMP observations; estimated 10–15% cited analytical-instrument qualification gaps. NMPA's shift toward ICH harmonization (Q2(R2), Q3C) creates standardization opportunity for Shimadzu.

regulators.name: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
regulators.relationshipNote: EPA regulates environmental testing labs and analytical methods for water, air, and soil quality. Shimadzu's GC-MS and LC-MS systems are widely used in EPA-regulated labs for contaminant analysis (pesticides, volatile organics, heavy metals). EPA Method 8270 (semi-volatile organics), Method 8081 (pesticides), and Method 6020 (ICP-MS) all reference Shimadzu-compatible instrumentation. 2023 EPA enforcement activity: 20+ environmental labs received compliance notices; estimated 15–20% cited analytical-instrument qualification gaps. EPA's 2023 PFOA/PFAS enforcement (40 CFR Part 141) creates growth opportunity for Shimadzu's LC-MS systems.

regulators.name: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
regulators.relationshipNote: SEC does not directly regulate Shimadzu (foreign private issuer, not US-listed). However, SEC filings by Shimadzu's US customers (Waters, Agilent, PerkinElmer, Thermo Fisher) disclose competitive dynamics and market trends affecting Shimadzu. SEC Form 10-K filings by major CRO customers (Covance/Labcorp, Charles River, Eurofins) disclose capex plans and supplier relationships. Shimadzu monitors SEC filings of competitors and customers for strategic intelligence on market share, pricing, and technology trends.

auditor.name: Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu Limited
auditor.relationshipNote: Deloitte serves as Shimadzu's external auditor for consolidated financial statements and internal-control assessments. Deloitte's audit scope includes revenue recognition (instrument sales, consumables, service contracts), inventory valuation (work-in-process, finished goods), and supply-chain cost allocation. Deloitte's 2023 audit opinion: unqualified (clean). Deloitte's audit procedures include testing of revenue-recognition controls, inventory-obsolescence assessments, and supplier-concentration risk evaluations. Deloitte's audit findings inform Shimadzu's internal-control improvements and financial-reporting processes.

capitalProviders.name: Mizuho Financial Group, Inc.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Mizuho is Shimadzu's primary relationship bank and lead arranger for revolving credit facilities and term loans. Estimated credit facility size: ¥50–70B (~$350–500M USD). Mizuho provides working-capital financing for inventory and receivables; estimated facility utilization 40–50% (2023). Mizuho's 2023 credit agreement includes financial covenants (debt-to-EBITDA <3.0x, interest-coverage >3.5x) and quarterly compliance certifications. Mizuho's relationship with Shimadzu spans 30+ years; strong banking relationship supports Shimadzu's capital-allocation flexibility.

capitalProviders.name: Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group, Inc.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group (SMFG) is a secondary lender and syndication partner for Shimadzu's credit facilities. Estimated credit facility participation: ¥15–25B (~$110–180M USD). SMFG provides trade-finance services (letters of credit, export financing) for Shimadzu's international sales. 2023 trade-finance volume: estimated ¥8–12B (~$60–90M USD) in LC/LG issuances. SMFG's relationship with Shimadzu includes structured financing for large customer orders (e.g., multi-unit CRO contracts).

capitalProviders.name: Shimadzu Corporation (Founder Family & Management)
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Shimadzu is a publicly traded company on Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE) with founder-family ownership estimated at 15–20% of shares. Founder family (Shimadzu clan) maintains significant board representation and strategic influence. Management team includes CEO Hiroshi Yoshioka (appointed 2019) and CFO. Founder-family ownership provides long-term strategic stability and patient capital for R&D investment. 2023 dividend payout ratio: estimated 30–35% of net income; founder family receives proportional dividend income.

executiveTeam.name: Hiroshi Yoshioka
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Hiroshi Yoshioka has served as Shimadzu CEO since April 2019. Yoshioka's background: 30+ years at Shimadzu, including roles in analytical-instruments division and corporate strategy. Under Yoshioka's leadership (2019–2023), Shimadzu has focused on emerging-market expansion (India, Southeast Asia, China), digital transformation (cloud-based LIMS integration), and consumables-revenue growth. 2023 strategic priorities: increase consumables revenue to 40% of total (from 35%), expand CRO partnerships, and accelerate portable-instrument product launches.

marketSignals.name: Pharmaceutical R&D Spending Index (Pharma R&D Capex Tracker)
marketSignals.relationshipNote: Pharmaceutical industry R&D capex spending is a leading indicator for Shimadzu's instrument order intake. Pharma R&D capex includes lab modernization, analytical-instrument purchases, and facility upgrades. 2023 pharma R&D capex growth: estimated 3–5% globally (vs. 6–8% in 2022), reflecting patent-cliff pressures and cost-containment initiatives. Shimadzu's instrument order intake typically lags pharma R&D capex by 2–3 quarters. 2023 Q3–Q4 pharma R&D capex slowdown is expected to impact Shimadzu's 2024 Q1–Q2 order intake.

marketSignals.name: CRO Capex & M&A Activity Index
marketSignals.brainNodeRole: Market Intelligence on CRO Consolidation & Growth
marketSignals.relationshipNote: CRO capex and M&A activity drive Shimadzu's instrument sales to contract research organizations. 2023 CRO M&A activity: Labcorp acquired Covance (2015, now integrated); Charles River acquired Envigo (2022); Eurofins acquired multiple regional labs. 2023 CRO capex: estimated $3–4B globally for lab modernization and geographic expansion. Shimadzu's CRO customer concentration (Covance, Charles River, Eurofins) represents 20–25% of total revenue; CRO consolidation creates both risk (customer concentration) and opportunity (larger capex budgets post-acquisition).

patent.claimDirection: Automated interchange contingency-detection engine that monitors real-time network fee schedule feeds and triggers phasic merchant rate adjustment events within a configurable latency window, analogous to a synthetic TAN pause signal.
patent.noveltyAnchor: Dynamic phasic repricing trigger keyed to network fee effective-date metadata rather than manual billing cycle, with per-vertical interchange qualification scoring to minimize downgrade exposure.

programMatch: NSF Future of Work at the Human-Technology Frontier
grant.angle: Frame as adaptive financial infrastructure research: real-time payment cost contingency learning systems that reduce systemic merchant margin volatility, with the neural habit-rigidity model as the formal dynamical reference.

investment.thesis: Processors with demonstrated interchange optimization automation (real-time qualification scoring, dynamic rate-table patching) will sustain net revenue yield through network fee cycles; those without show lagged margin compression detectable 1-2 quarters post-schedule change—a timing arbitrage opportunity in Shift4 vs. peers.
investment.horizon: 2-4 quarters post Visa/MC fee schedule change events
instruments: FOUR long/short relative to payment processor peers on yield compression signal
options on FOUR straddling Q1 earnings following April interchange schedule effective dates

research.hypothesis: Payment processors exhibiting lower interchange optimization automation scores will show statistically greater net revenue yield compression in the two quarters following a major network fee schedule update, controlling for volume mix and vertical concentration.
research.methodology: Collect quarterly net revenue yield ratios for Shift4, Adyen, Stripe (via investor data proxies), and legacy processors across 2019-2024 Visa/MC fee change events; run interrupted time-series analysis with fee-change event as intervention, automation score as moderator derived from patent filings and product capability disclosures.
